justification: Formed a fresh judgment of the whole article, then checked the round-1 fix and re-verified primary sources myself rather than trusting the prior review. Round 1 capped the score at 7.0 for an unscoped 'only' claim — that generation 2 is 'scanned only when the younger generations can't free enough memory on their own' — which the Fundamentals page's own 'Conditions for a garbage collection' section contradicted by listing a low-memory notification and an explicit GC.Collect() call as independent triggers. I re-fetched that exact section fresh this round. It lists three conditions verbatim: low physical memory (OS notification or host-indicated), the allocated-object threshold being surpassed, and an explicit GC.Collect() call. The rewrite ('That cascade is the common path, not the only one: ... also lists a low-memory notification ... and an explicit GC.Collect() call, as independent triggers') accurately reflects two of those three conditions and correctly drops the false 'only'. Both of round 1's minor issues are also fixed and I independently re-verified the fixes: the GC.CollectionCount 'at least that generation' claim now cites the Fundamentals line 'collecting a generation means collecting objects in that generation and all its younger generations' (present, verbatim, on the live page), and the cache/WeakReference paragraph now quotes the Weak References page's actual caveat ('avoid using weak references as an automatic solution to memory management problems ... instead, develop an effective caching policy') instead of overselling it as 'exactly this case' (I re-fetched that page too; the quote and the tree-view example are both accurate). I also independently re-verified, against freshly fetched pages, every other quoted claim I could cheaply spot-check: the DI-disposal line and 'doesn't allocate or release unmanaged memory' line from Implementing Dispose, the 'at least two garbage collections' line from Object.Finalize, and that GC.Collect() with no arguments 'forces an immediate garbage collection of all generations' per its own API page — all match verbatim. The one thing I could not fully substantiate is a smaller, softer version of the same class of problem round 1 flagged: the rewritten sentence attaches 'as independent triggers that can force a full sweep of every generation' to the Conditions section for both the low-memory trigger and the GC.Collect() call, but that section itself never states which generation gets collected under any of its three conditions — it only lists when 'a garbage collection' happens. The 'full sweep' claim is independently true and separately cited for GC.Collect() (verified via the GC.Collect API page's own remarks), but for the low-memory-notification trigger specifically, nothing I fetched from Microsoft Learn confirms it always results in a full (generation 2) collection rather than some other generation. This is a citation-precision nit — hedged with 'can' rather than asserted as universal, and not contradicted by any source the way the round-1 'only' claim was — not a demonstrated factual error, so it does not trigger the 7.0 cap, but it keeps the article from a clean 9+. I also verified the new 'Prove it' exercise's reported gotcha myself: compiling and running a standalone program that constructs `new WeakReference(cache[0])` (the List indexer passed directly as the constructor argument) reproduces `IsAlive: True` even after `cache.Clear()`, `GC.Collect()` and `GC.WaitForPendingFinalizers()` on this machine, while the article's actual fix — assigning to a local `object? item`, nulling it, then collecting — correctly reproduces `before: True` / `after: False`. The exercise's solution code is accurate and the underlying gotcha is real and reproducible, not invented. `node tools/run-code.mjs src/content/articles/csharp-dotnet/garbage-collection.md` passes clean (35 blocks, 18 executed — up two exercises' worth from round 1's 33/17, consistent with the new exercise). Against the two ranking third-party pages, this article is unambiguously deeper: neither covers IDisposable-vs-finalizer, weak references, or the event-handler-leak mechanism, and neither has a single compiled/measured code sample, let alone 18 of them with real output. Against Microsoft's own Fundamentals page — the best existing result for this query — the article now covers the same ground plus the IDisposable/finalizer split, weak references, and leak diagnosis that Microsoft spreads across several separate pages, and it demonstrates nearly every claim with runnable code rather than asserting it in prose, while remaining accurate to what those pages say (modulo the one citation nit above). That is 8.5-anchor territory (MDN/Real Python-equal, nits only) with real added rigor over the anchor's baseline, landing at 8.6.
